title: Walking the Camino
hookLine: hundreds of thousands walk to Santiago every year

lines: TWO WORDS ON A DUSTY ROAD.
A STAMP IN A LITTLE BOOKLET.
cards: Buen camino. Two words, called across a dusty road in northern Spain. A farmer leaning on a gate says it to a passing walker with a backpack.

Two strangers share a bench by a fountain, and as one heaves the pack back on, the other says it. A woman behind a café counter hands over a coffee, presses an ink stamp into a little booklet, and says it too.
In Spanish it means something like good way, or good road. And this road leads to a cathedral in a city called Santiago de Compostela.

teach.b: The Camino de Santiago means the Way of Saint James. Back in year three, pilgrims' roads passed through Santiago. Tradition says the apostle James is buried there, and walkers come along several routes.
Some start at their own front doors. Some walk for prayer, some for grief, some to think, some without being sure why. Next, that word, way.
In John's Gospel, Jesus says, "I am the way, the truth, and the life."
In Acts, before the name Christian shows up, Saul goes looking for followers of Jesus, "that if he found any of this way, whether they were men or women, he might bring them bound unto Jerusalem."
The early followers were people of the Way, and for some walkers, wishing a stranger a good way carries that echo.

teach.h: A STRANGER ON THE EMMAUS ROAD.
teach.b: Then Emmaus. On the day of the resurrection, two heartbroken disciples walk out of Jerusalem. "Jesus himself drew near, and went with them."
They don't know him. He walks, listens, and opens the scriptures to them. At the village, evening coming on, they beg him: "Abide with us: for it is toward evening, and the day is far spent."
At supper he breaks the bread, they know him, and he's gone. "Did not our heart burn within us, while he talked with us by the way?"
Last, the greeting. Some walkers say you don't choose your companions: the stranger who shares water or a bandage may be the one you remember.
Catholics, Protestants, Orthodox Christians and people unsure what they believe walk the same road, and buen camino doesn't ask which.

how: Pilgrims walk the Camino de Santiago on several routes across Spain and beyond, carrying a pilgrim's booklet stamped along the way, and some attend the pilgrims' Mass at the cathedral in Santiago when they arrive.

o: a hiking trail across Spain with no religious past
the pilgrim road to Santiago, the Way of Saint James
a procession around a cathedral on a saint's day

s: the Camino is one single road
walkers come to Santiago along several routes, and some start at their own front doors.
in Acts, the followers of Jesus are called people of "this way"
Saul hunts for "any of this way, whether they were men or women."
the two on the Emmaus road knew Jesus at once
they knew him only at supper, when he broke the bread.

games.q: you're walking to Emmaus, heartbroken. a stranger has walked with you all afternoon and opened the scriptures. at the village he makes as if to go on. what do you do?
o: say goodbye at the edge of the village.
beg him to stay and eat with you.
walk faster to be rid of him.
games.why: "Abide with us: for it is toward evening." at supper he breaks the bread, and they know him.

practice: Stand and walk slowly around the room, one step for each breath, heel, then ball, then toes; if you can't stand, press each foot into the floor in turn.
If you pray, you can pray with your steps, a word from a psalm or the name of someone you're carrying; if you don't, count the steps and notice the feet that carry you.

wordCard.voice: Walking the Camino. The pilgrim road to Santiago, the Way of Saint James, where walkers wish each other buen camino.

orig.note: Greek: way, road. the word in John 14:6, "I am the way," and in Acts for the people of the Way.

carryVoice: Your line: buen camino. A good way, wished to whoever walks beside you. Rest well.
